title: Don't wait to be rich
hookLine: many would have reached wisdom if they hadn't thought they'd need to be rich first

cards: Once the kids are older. Once I pay off the card. Once work calms down.
Once I have the right shoes, the right desk, the right app. Then I'll start. Plenty of plans hang on a sentence like that, and the thing they're waiting for keeps moving.
Lucilius had one too. He told Seneca he'd devote himself to philosophy properly once he'd put enough money aside to live on. Seneca's seventeenth letter is his reply, and it's not gentle.

teach.b: Lucilius wants to build up savings before giving himself to the study of how to live. Sounds sensible. Seneca tells him to throw that plan out.
If you're wise, hurry toward a sound mind now. Riches, he says, have shut many people off from wisdom. They meant to get rich first and study how to live afterward, and the afterward never came.
The getting-ready becomes the whole life; the money always needs a little more.
Then he praises a poor person's freedom. When the war trumpet sounds, the poor know they aren't the ones under attack. When a house is on fire, they look for the way out, not for what to carry.
When a poor person sets out to sea, no crowd of servants fills the dock. Hunger costs little; fussiness costs a lot. Nature asks for very little.
If you want room for your mind, either be poor, or live as if you were. He closes with Epicurus again: for many, getting rich didn't end their troubles; it only changed them.
The study of wisdom, Seneca says, can't do you good without care for simple living, and simple living is a poverty you choose.
That choice is open on any budget: a notebook instead of a course, a walk instead of a gym, five quiet minutes instead of a retreat.

how: Following Seneca, some people begin a practice of reflection or study right away with simple means, rather than waiting for savings, time off or better conditions.

practice: Name one thing you've been waiting to begin until conditions are right, and what you've told yourself you need first. Then ask what you could do with exactly what you have, today, and make it tiny: one page, one call, one stretch.
Notice how small the first step really is.
